clinician.trajectory_summary: A 57-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes on benazepril (started approximately 4 months prior) presented to the ED with acute onset tongue swelling, dysphonia, and dyspnea on the morning of presentation. He had received multiple IM epinephrine doses in the prehospital setting without improvement. Physical examination revealed pronounced lingual and perioral edema without urticaria, pruritus, or pain, with preserved airway patency (SpO2 96% on room air) but decreased bilateral breath sounds with inspiratory effort and tachycardia. Laboratory workup showed mild leucocytosis (10.8×10⁹/L), lymphopenia (800×10⁹/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (hsCRP 7.80 mg/dL, ferritin 866 ng/mL, LDH 1295 IU/L). In the ED, tranexamic acid was administered with clinical improvement over 3 hours. The patient was admitted for airway monitoring and received IV diphenhydramine and famotidine; benazepril was withheld. Angioedema resolved within 24 hours. He was discharged on oral diphenhydramine and famotidine, with amlodipine substituted for benazepril. A nasopharyngeal swab for COVID-19 PCR was obtained on admission, and the result returned positive soon after discharge, confirming concomitant COVID-19 infection.
